claims.text: Spin-polarized DFT augmented with local spin fluctuation treatments can identify and predict ferromagnetic ground states in transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys.
The DFT+LSF method captures both itinerant and local-moment behavior of d-electrons.
Equiatomic Fe-Cr-Co-Ni can be considered a chemically disordered BCC or FCC solid solution at low temperature.
LSF calculations can use root-mean-square magnetic moments to represent longitudinal spin-fluctuation energetics.
The fluctuating medium approximation and one-shot-from-static-equilibrium approach can be used to determine the magnetic moments required by the LSF treatment.
The method can compare the energetic stability of ferromagnetic and non-magnetic configurations.
The calculations should be performed at 0 K to compare ground states.
Finite-temperature calculations can include magnetic entropy contributions.
Typical DFT exchange-correlation functionals are suitable for these calculations.
The relevant structural mediator is the set of local magnetic moments on d-electron sites.
Exchange interactions captured by the LSF framework mediate alignment of the local moments.
Explicit treatment of longitudinal spin fluctuations allows assessment of the energetic preference for aligned ferromagnetic moment configurations.
A ferromagnetic state will have lower total energy when exchange interactions dominate over thermal disorder.
For the stated alloy and conditions, DFT+LSF will predict a ferromagnetic state with lower energy than a non-magnetic or disordered-local-moment state.
The calculated energetic preference will correlate with experimentally observable ferromagnetic behavior.
DFT without LSF may describe finite-temperature magnetic effects less accurately.
DFT without LSF could miss ferromagnetic ordering when local fluctuations are important.
The method is most applicable to alloys with significant d-electron contributions.
Predictions are limited by the choice of density functional and treatment of electron correlations.
A consistent prediction of a ferromagnetic ground state for alloys experimentally found to have non-magnetic or paramagnetic ground states would falsify the claimed reliability of the method.
